text: This is Earth. You are about to leave it, headed for the most dangerous object in the universe.
A black hole: a place where gravity is so strong that space itself folds shut around it.
Our ship points at a quiet one, thirty times the mass of the Sun, floating in the dark.
From far away you would not see it at all. No surface, no glow. Just the stars, sliding out of place.
Get closer, and the sky begins to bend. Light from stars behind it wraps around into a perfect ring.
That glowing disk is real: gas superheated to millions of degrees, spiralling in at half the speed of light.
Then comes the strangest part. Gravity pulls harder at your feet than at your head.
Fall feet first, and the hole stretches you like spaghetti. Physicists really call it that.
Cross the line we call the event horizon, and to you, nothing happens. No wall. No flash.
But you can never come back. To return, you would have to fly faster than light itself.
And for the people watching from outside? Your clock slows down. You fade, redder and dimmer, and freeze.
To them, you never quite arrive. To you, the fall feels almost gentle.
Inside, everything falls toward the centre, and the centre is a place called a singularity.
Not a thing. A place where the known laws of physics simply give up.
Here, space and time trade places. Point yourself anywhere. Every direction leads down.
In a fraction of a second the tides grow infinite, and you become part of the hole.
So how long does it last? From the outside, maybe forever. But not quite.
Black holes slowly evaporate. A faint glow, called Hawking radiation, leaks away across unimaginable ages.
In the end the hole vanishes, and everything it ever knew leaks back into the universe as light.
You never get there. And yet, in a way, everything does.
